title: What Global Commons Trusts Is
definition: Global Commons Trusts: trusts holding the global commons.
description:
Strip Global Commons Trusts to its essence and you get trusts holding the global commons. Simple to say, civilizational to build.

The path runs through Future Governance & Society: first commons charters understanding, then trust logistics prototypes, then trustee duties operations at scale. Each stage has its own physics, its own economics, and its own failure modes — this database maps all three.

Use the ladder: start with foundations, work through the components and forecasts, run every demo, then attempt the compounded drills. By the final record you will hold a working mental model of trust hulls, grounded in real research and honest about what remains unknown.

t: Real Research Today: Global Commons Trusts
title: Real Research Today: Global Commons Trusts
definition: Today's documented research behind Global Commons Trusts.
description:
The road to Global Commons Trusts is already being paved. The Artemis Accords (30+ signatories) set norms for lunar and space governance. The Network State literature (Balaji Srinivasan) theorizes cloud-first political communities.

Participatory budgeting (Porto Alegre origin) now runs in 3,000+ cities worldwide. Together these programs form the commons charters foundation that Global Commons Trusts will build on — the trust logistics results, the trustee duties methods, and the institutional memory.

Forecasts are projections, not promises: the dated milestones in this database reflect published roadmaps and expert surveys, and they will move as trust logistics research advances. Treat every date as a planning scenario with error bars, and watch the signals listed in each milestone record.

t: 2030 — First trust hulls charter ratified: commons charters deliberatio

title: Readiness Estimator: Global Commons Trusts
definition: Estimates Global Commons Trusts readiness from component maturity.
description:
The estimator scores the six Global Commons Trusts components on the TRL 1–9 scale and averages them into a verdict: research phase, pilot phase, or deployment phase. Scores derive from the component records in this database — change a component's maturity and the verdict moves.

Honest scoring is the point: a trust hulls that averages TRL 3 is not failing, it is three phases from deployment, and the estimator tells you which component drags the average down. Fund that one first.

title: Global Commons Trusts Systems Simulator
definition: Simulates Global Commons Trusts operating for a day.
description:
The simulator walks a Global Commons Trusts installation through six operating steps, with seeded randomness standing in for real-world variation. Seed 50312 reproduces this exact run — change the seed in the program to explore other days.

Watch for DEGRADED steps: they mark where commons charters monitoring, trust logistics redundancy, or trustee duties maintenance would intervene in a real deployment. A simulator that never degrades is lying; this one degrades about eight percent of the time, like early hardware does.

title: Global Commons Trusts Master Roadmap
definition: The united roadmap for Global Commons Trusts: prove, build, operate, compound.
description:
The master roadmap for Global Commons Trusts — trusts holding the global commons.

Phase 1 — Prove (commons charters): laboratory demonstrations of every component, replicated independently. No scaling until the physics is boring.

Phase 2 — Build (trust logistics): pilot manufacturing and integration. The six pieces meet for the first time and the interfaces get honest.

Phase 3 — Operate (trustee duties): continuous real-world operation. Uptime, cost curves and failure data replace projections.

Phase 4 — Compound (benefit sharing): trust hulls as everyday infrastructure. Costs collapse, standards settle, and Earth-scale deployment begins.

Public edition: phases follow documented research readiness. This record unites the database: overview, research, components, milestones, demos and drills all point here.
